title: The Chip Deal That Sealed It: Inside India and the Netherlands' New Strategic Partnership
excerpt: PM Modi's Hague visit produced 17 agreements, a landmark semiconductor pact with ASML, and a signal that New Delhi is diversifying its tech alliances beyond Washington
body:
When Prime Minister Narendra Modi landed in The Hague on 16 May for the second leg of his five-nation tour, the visit was framed as a diplomatic courtesy call on a mid-sized European ally. By the time he left, India and the Netherlands had signed 17 bilateral agreements, elevated their relationship to a full strategic partnership, and locked in what may prove to be the most consequential semiconductor deal in Indian industrial history.

The centrepiece is a partnership between Tata Electronics and ASML, the Dutch firm that holds a near-monopoly on the extreme ultraviolet lithography machines without which no cutting-edge chip can be manufactured. The agreement clears the path for an $11 billion front-end semiconductor fabrication facility in Dholera, Gujarat — India's first genuine entry into the top tier of global chipmaking.

## Why the Netherlands matters now

For decades, India's strategic attention in Europe has been trained on London, Paris, and Berlin. The Netherlands, despite being India's fourth-largest trading partner in the EU with bilateral trade touching $27.8 billion last year, rarely featured in the foreign-policy conversation. That changed when the global chip supply chain became a theatre of geopolitical competition.

ASML's lithography systems are indispensable. The United States has pressured the Dutch government to restrict exports of its most advanced machines to China. India, which has largely been a spectator in the semiconductor wars, saw an opening. The Dholera fab, backed by Tata's industrial muscle and ASML's technology, is designed to produce chips for automotive, telecom, and defence applications — sectors where India currently imports nearly everything.

Dutch Prime Minister Rob Jetten, who took office earlier this year, was eager to reciprocate. "India is not just a market," he said at a joint press conference. "It is a partner in building resilient supply chains." The two leaders also announced a digital sea corridor for green hydrogen between Rotterdam and Gujarat, a dairy research centre, and expanded cooperation in water management — an area where the Netherlands, much of which sits below sea level, has centuries of expertise.

## The diaspora dimension

Modi addressed a packed Indian community event in The Hague, where an estimated 45,000 people of Indian origin live in the Netherlands. The Dutch Indian diaspora, though smaller than those in the UK or the US, punches above its weight in technology, finance, and academia. Several Indian-origin professionals hold senior positions at ASML, Philips, and ING Bank.

For NRIs watching from abroad, the semiconductor pact carries a more personal resonance. India's chip ambitions could, over time, create a reverse brain-drain pipeline — drawing back engineers and managers who cut their teeth at TSMC, Intel, or Samsung. The Dholera fab alone is projected to generate 20,000 direct jobs and several multiples of that in ancillary employment.

## What comes next

The strategic partnership commits both countries to annual foreign-minister consultations, a defence dialogue, and a joint working group on artificial intelligence. A free-trade agreement between India and the EU, long stalled, now has the Netherlands as an active champion.

The real test, however, will be execution. India's semiconductor programme has been announced before — most notably in 2022 — with limited results. The ASML partnership adds credibility, but Dholera's fab must navigate India's infrastructure bottlenecks, power supply challenges, and the sheer complexity of chip manufacturing, where a single speck of dust can ruin a wafer worth thousands of dollars.

Modi, characteristically, was bullish. "This is not just a trade relationship," he told Dutch CEOs at a roundtable. "This is a partnership to design and manufacture the future." Whether that future arrives on schedule will depend on whether India can match its diplomatic ambition with industrial discipline.
